Where it began

Stuart Binny was born in Bangalore on 3 June 1984, and cricket was the family business. His father, Roger Binny, had played Test cricket for India, and for a while Roger was also the cricket coach at St Joseph's Indian High School, where Stuart went after The Frank Anthony Public School. There was further coaching at IACA under Imtiaz Ahmed.

He first played for Karnataka in 2003/04. Holding a regular place in the first-class side took time, and he came to think of himself mainly as a limited-overs cricketer.

The player

The longer game came round to him all the same. His 20 wickets in the 2011–12 Ranji Trophy cost only 20.10 each, and ten came in a single match against Odisha. In the Indian Premier League he turned out for Mumbai Indians, Rajasthan Royals and Royal Challengers Bangalore, and was often the man sent in to rescue an innings or finish a chase.

His Test debut came in England in 2014. He made one in the first innings and 78 in the second, which remained his best. In all he played 6 Tests between 2014 and 2015, scoring 194 runs at 21.56 and taking 3 wickets, with a best of 2 for 24. He also played one-day and Twenty20 internationals, making his T20 debut against Zimbabwe on 17 July 2015.

What made him special

On 17 June 2014 against Bangladesh he had the kind of day most bowlers only imagine: six wickets for four runs. It moved him past Anil Kumble as the owner of India's best one-day figures, and the record stood until Mohammad Shami's seven wickets at the 2023 World Cup.

His three Test wickets were hard-won, at 86.00 each, but he was a useful hitter and a handy bowler, the sort of all-rounder captains like to have around. He was picked in the squad for the 2015 World Cup and watched it from close quarters without playing a game.

Away from the middle

Later in his career he moved from Karnataka to Nagaland for the 2019–20 Ranji Trophy season, and on 30 August 2021 he retired from every form of the game. He went on to play in the Legends League Cricket, for Gujarat Giants in the first season and Urbanrisers Hyderabad in the second.

And finally

In 2019 he looked back on his career in a piece for the Hindustan Times, giving it the title Almost Famous: A life in cricket. A man who once took six wickets for four runs in an international match was perhaps being a little modest.
